letters.headline: Seventy-one per cent of the average, and counting
paragraphs: Your piece on the education budget says a teacher earns about 2,300 som against an average wage of 3,250. I have taught English at School No. 31 since 1993 and I can tell you the percentage feels smaller at the market than it looks in print.

What the story does not say is what the 1,400 vacant posts look like from inside a school. In our staff room we do not lose English teachers to the ministry's difficulties, we lose them to the bazaar, to Almaty and to jobs where a dollar wage is paid. A colleague of mine in a district school teaches English, and some weeks also covers a physics class because nobody else will. She does not complain, she simply marks both sets of copybooks at home.

The Ministry says pay is "set in som and paid in som". True. But the bread, the potatoes and the winter boots are bought by the same teachers who are told this. I would ask only that the education chapter, when it comes, be printed as a line with a number in it, not a promise.
Our children learn English from us. We would like to be able to afford to stay.
letters.name: Gulzat Mambetova

letters.headline: Who writes down a bus's diesel?
paragraphs: I read the story on fuel sales tax with the interest of a man who fills a bus. Pump prices have not moved, so I agree that the 9 per cent must come from somewhere else. The tax service says more litres declared and more audits. Good. But how many litres? How many audits? The release does not say, and I would like to know, because every driver I know takes a receipt at the pump for the company and always has.

The Ministry's man says diesel carried up to the Chatkal villages in cans has no receipt behind it. I believe him. In the villages the price is 8.55 to 9.75 a litre, against 6.10 at NurGaz, and a family does not carry a can that distance for the pleasure of it.

On my own road, over the Fergana Gateway, the pass is open today with chains or winter tyres required, and the diesel I burn climbing it is the best-recorded litre in the country. Perhaps the tax service might spare a thought for those of us who are counted every day, and tell us how many of the others it has found.
letters.name: Ulan Bekov
letters.reply: The Herald has asked the State Tax Service for the litres sold and the number of station audits behind the 9 per cent. It had not replied by press time.

letters.headline: Smoke behind the Dastgoh market at six
paragraphs: Your editorial on Nurzhan's air asks what is burning. I cannot give you a study, only what I see from my fourth-floor window in Dastgoh, where I have lived for thirty-one years.

In the mornings, before the market opens, there is a low brown smoke from behind the rows of kiosks, and it does not smell like coal. It smells like plastic and wet cardboard. I do not know who lights it or whether it is the same every day. I am not accusing anyone, I only say that if the city does not know how many tonnes of rubbish it collects, it cannot know how many are being burned instead of collected.

On the day the reading was 196 my granddaughter walked to school in a scarf over her mouth, and her teacher told the class to keep the windows shut at break. That is the plan, for now. I would like the Administration to count the bins before it counts the excuses.
Please keep asking. Nobody here reads the numbers from Gidromet, but everybody reads the sky.
letters.name: Tamara Ilyina
letters.reply: Nurzhan City Administration has still published no figure for the refuse it collects. The Herald will put Ms Ilyina's question to it again.

letters.headline: Mr Kurbanov is more than a post office
paragraphs: I am 71 and made my own Umrah by road through Tashkent twelve years ago, so the story of the forty pilgrims in the hostel touched me. I will say two things.

First, to anyone in the Rim planning a pilgrimage: before you hand over your money, ask to see the booking for the whole journey, not only the first leg, and ask for it in writing. A good operator will not mind. Ours was a decent man, and it still took two letters to get his paper.

Second, Imam Abdulla Kurbanov told your reporter, "I am a post office, not a travel agent." That is modest. In Bazar-Korgon we know he has sat up with the families' phone calls and the dollar worries. Families are buying dollars at nearly twelve som, and that is a lot of money for a village, to pay for hostel beds in another country.
I pray the group flies soon and that the families are not left to carry the bill alone. We have always looked after our own on the Rim, and this is a time to do it.
letters.name: Abdurahim Sultanov
